questions.q: How do the Apache Kafka Java clients expose their metrics by default?

options.t: Through a built-in HTTP endpoint on port 9090
options.why: The clients don't run an HTTP server for metrics.

options.t: Only in the broker's metrics, never in the client
options.why: Clients have their own metrics registry.

options.t: In a dedicated metrics topic the client writes every minute
options.why: The clients don't write metrics to a topic by default.

questions.explain: The Java clients use Kafka Metrics and expose metrics via JMX, with pluggable reporters for other monitoring systems.

questions.q: A dashboard shows `records-consumed-rate`. Which metric gives the cumulative count of records consumed?

options.why: The cumulative partner has the -total suffix.
The cumulative partner has the -total suffix.

options.t: There is none; only rates are recorded
options.why: Every rate metric has a -total partner.

questions.explain: All Kafka rate metrics have a corresponding cumulative count metric with the suffix `-total`.

questions.q: What does the consumer metric `records-lag-max` measure?

options.t: The largest record lag of any partition, from the current position
The time since the oldest unconsumed record was produced
The lag from the last committed offset, summed over all partitions
options.why: It's based on the current offset, not the committed one, and is a maximum.

options.t: The highest offset the producer has written
options.why: That's the log-end offset, not lag.

questions.explain: `records-lag-max` is the maximum lag in records for any partition in the window, based on the current offset, not the committed offset.

questions.q: `kafka-consumer-groups --describe` shows lag of 5 000 on a partition, but the consumer's `records-lag` metric shows 200. What explains it?

options.t: The metric counts bytes, the tool counts records
One of them must be broken
The tool also counts records in transactions that haven't committed yet
options.why: The difference comes from position versus committed offset.

options.t: The tool uses the committed offset; the metric the current position

questions.explain: The group tool shows lag from the group's committed offset; the client metric is based on the consumer's current position, which runs ahead of commits.

questions.q: According to the Kafka monitoring docs, which TWO consumer conditions show it is keeping up?

options.why: Zero idle means the consumer is always busy, not necessarily keeping up.

options.t: assigned-partitions equal to the partition count
options.why: That depends on group size, not on keeping up.
High commit latency isn't a health signal.

questions.explain: For a consumer to keep up, max lag needs to be less than a threshold and min fetch rate needs to be larger than 0.

questions.q: Consumers keep getting removed from their group for being slow. Which metric shows how close they get to `max.poll.interval.ms`?

options.why: That measures fetch requests, not the gap between polls.

options.t: heartbeat-rate, which drops when polls slow down
options.why: Heartbeats continue even when polls are slow.
A rate doesn't show the gap between polls.

questions.explain: `time-between-poll-max` is the max delay between `poll()` calls; when it nears `max.poll.interval.ms`, members get removed.

questions.q: A consumer's `poll-idle-ratio-avg` is close to 0. What does that suggest?

options.t: The consumer spends most of its time waiting for new data to arrive
options.why: That would be a high idle ratio.

options.t: The broker is throttling the consumer
Its user code processing records takes almost all the time
The consumer has no partitions assigned

questions.explain: `poll-idle-ratio-avg` is the fraction of time `poll()` is idle rather than waiting for user code to process records: near 0 means processing dominates.

questions.q: An alert should fire when a consumer has stopped calling `poll()`. Which metric fits best?

options.why: Lead measures distance from the start of the log.
Connections can stay open while poll isn't called.
It can be zero simply because no data arrives.

questions.explain: `last-poll-seconds-ago` is the number of seconds since the last `poll()` invocation.

questions.q: Which consumer metrics show how long rebalances take and whether they fail?

options.t: fetch-latency-avg and fetch-rate, from the fetch manager

questions.explain: The coordinator metrics include `rebalance-latency-avg`, `failed-rebalance-total` and `last-rebalance-seconds-ago`.

questions.q: To check how many partitions a single consumer instance owns right now, which metric is used?
questions.explain: `assigned-partitions` (consumer-coordinator-metrics) is the number of partitions currently assigned to the consumer.

questions.q: Which producer metric shows sends that ended in errors?

options.why: Retries may still succeed; errors are counted separately.

questions.explain: `record-error-rate` is the average per-second number of record sends that resulted in errors; `record-retry-rate` counts retried sends.

questions.q: `record-retry-rate` climbs during a broker restart but `record-error-rate` stays at 0. What does that show?

options.t: Records are being lost silently, without any error being counted
options.why: Errors would be counted; none were.
Retries mean it is still sending.

questions.explain: Retriable errors (such as a leader change) are retried by the producer; if retries succeed within `delivery.timeout.ms`, no send ends in an error.

questions.q: A producer's `send()` calls start blocking. `buffer-available-bytes` is near zero and `bufferpool-wait-ratio` is high. What is happening?

options.t: The record accumulator is full, so send() waits for buffer space
The broker is rejecting the producer's records as too large to store
options.why: That would show as errors, not buffer waits.

questions.explain: When `buffer.memory` is used up, `send()` blocks up to `max.block.ms`. `buffer-available-bytes` shows free buffer memory and `bufferpool-wait-ratio` the time spent waiting for it.

questions.q: End-to-end latency is high. Which producer metric shows how long batches wait in the send buffer before being sent?

options.why: That measures the request once sent.
That's the I/O thread's idle time.

questions.explain: `record-queue-time-avg` is the average time record batches spent in the send buffer; `request-latency-avg` covers the request itself.

questions.q: A team raised `linger.ms` to improve batching. Which TWO producer metrics show whether batches got bigger?
questions.explain: `batch-size-avg` is the average bytes sent per partition per request, and `records-per-request-avg` the average records per request.

questions.q: A producer uses zstd compression. What does a `compression-rate-avg` of 0.25 mean?

options.t: Only a quarter of the producer's batches were actually compressed
options.why: It's a ratio of sizes, not of batches.

options.t: Compressed batches are about a quarter of their original size

options.why: 0.25 means they shrank to a quarter.

options.t: The CPU spent 25% of its time compressing

questions.explain: `compression-rate-avg` is the average ratio of compressed batch size to uncompressed size.

questions.q: A producer's throughput is capped well below its usual rate, with no errors. `produce-throttle-time-avg` is high. What is the likely cause?

options.t: A failing disk on the producer's host
options.why: The producer doesn't write to its own disk.

options.t: Too many partitions in the topic
The brokers are throttling the producer's requests

questions.explain: `produce-throttle-time-avg` is the average time a request was throttled by a broker; consumers have `fetch-throttle-time-avg`.

questions.q: Several applications on one host each run a producer, and their metrics are hard to tell apart in JMX. What helps most?

options.t: Setting a meaningful client.id, which appears in the metric names
Using a different bootstrap.servers order per application

questions.explain: Client metrics are registered per `client-id` (for example `kafka.producer:type=producer-metrics,client-id=…`), so a meaningful `client.id` tells them apart.

questions.q: A consumer's fetch requests seem slow. Which metric measures them directly?
questions.explain: `fetch-latency-avg` is the average time taken for a fetch request; `fetch-rate` is fetch requests per second.

questions.q: A consumer reads a topic with short retention. Which metric warns that it is close to the start of the log, where records may be deleted before it reads them?

options.why: Lag measures distance from the end of the log.

questions.explain: `records-lead-min` is the minimum lead in records for any partition: how far the consumer is from the start of the log, which retention moves forward.

questions.q: Which metric shows the lag of one specific partition, rather than the maximum across partitions?

options.why: That is the maximum across partitions.

options.t: records-lag, tagged with topic and partition
fetch-rate divided by the number of assigned partitions

questions.explain: `records-lag` is reported per partition (`partition` and `topic` tags) with the partition's latest lag.
